A design challenge of using electric motors to drive propellers is that, for a given power, the speciﬁc power and/or eﬃciency of an electric motor increases as its tip speed increases whereas the propulsive eﬃciency of a propeller increases as its tip speed decreases. Consequently, directly driving the propeller with an electric motor requires a compromise in speed between the two and an optimization of the propeller-motor system. An alternative is to connect the motor to the propeller through a speed reducing gearbox. This approach adds complexity and potentially reduces reliability but permits the motor and propeller to be optimized individually. A second challenge with the direct drive approach is that when noise is a concern, the propeller’s tip speed must be reduced by slowing its rotation or reducing its diameter; in either case, the directly connected motor ends up occupying a larger fraction of the propeller’s cross-sectional area, which reduces propulsive eﬃciency. With a geared motor, this penalty can be avoided by increasing the gear ratio to reduce the propeller’s speed rather than decreasing the motor’s speed, which would require a commensurate increase in its rated torque and diameter. response.answer: A speed-reducing gearbox allows the motor and propeller to operate near their preferred speeds: electric-motor specific power and/or efficiency generally improve with higher tip speed, while propeller efficiency improves with lower tip speed. It also allows propeller speed to be reduced without slowing and enlarging the motor, helping avoid a propulsive-efficiency penalty when noise limits propeller tip speed. The tradeoff is added complexity and potentially lower reliability. Conventional mechanical gears additionally suffer losses, vibration-induced noise, tooth wear, possible tooth failure, and friction-related heating that requires lubrication; these drawbacks motivate consideration of magnetic gearing as an alternative. The supplied evidence does not provide further specific operating details for magnetic gears.

claims.text: For a given power, a speed-reducing gearbox lets the motor and propeller be optimized separately, reconciling the motor’s preference for higher speed with the propeller’s preference for lower tip speed. It can also reduce propeller speed without requiring a corresponding reduction in motor speed, torque rating increase, and diameter increase.

A geared drivetrain adds complexity and may reduce reliability, while conventional mechanically contacting gears cause energy loss, vibration-induced noise, tooth wear, possible tooth failure, and friction-induced heating; lubrication is required to limit friction and prevent heat-related gearbox failure. response.answer: PT-2 improved measured specific torque from 20 Nm/kg for PT-1 to a preliminary 44.7 Nm/kg—more than double—through several coordinated changes. Custom annular-wedge magnets reduced gaps between adjacent magnets, especially in the sun; a redesigned modulator containment structure reduced the modulator-to-ring gap; and the Halbach arrays produced greater specific flux by using six rather than four magnets per array along with radially thinner, circumferentially shorter, higher-pole-count arrays. Thinner pole pieces further improved flux coupling while reducing mass. Further improvement remains mechanically constrained because the minimum achievable magnetic gap is governed by the mechanical design, so features that permit thinner gaps are needed.

The Halbach arrays increased specific flux by changing from four to six magnets per array and using radially thinner, circumferentially shorter, higher-pole-count arrays.
Thinner pole pieces increased flux coupling and reduced mass, contributing to the specific-torque improvement.

response.answer: The thermal management system (TMS) was solved separately because solving the full electric aircraft propulsion (EAP) system simultaneously caused errors in the calculated electrical losses. Those errors directly affected the TMS fluid mass-flow and temperature calculations, making system convergence unstable. The core EAP system was therefore solved first, and the TMS was solved afterward using the resulting constant electrical losses. This sequencing greatly improved stability by decoupling the TMS calculation from changing electrical-loss values during convergence.

claims.text: Solving the full EAP system at once caused errors in the electrical losses, which propagated into the TMS fluid mass-flow and temperature calculations and destabilized convergence.

Multiple electric engines could fail during takeoff, either due to bus failure or bird strike. With the bus configuration described in Jansen et al. [9], a single bus failure causes loss of four electric engines, balanced across the aircraft with two failed electric engines on each wing, to reduce any adverse yaw or roll effect [9]. A bird strike could damage any number of electric engines on a given wing, from a single engine to all eight. Using the same calculations given in Section IV.B, the remaining electric engines and turbofan must be able to produce at least7.2 MW of energy to allow a safe takeoff. The loss of electric engine cases have been identified as an area of future work and analysis. D. Loss of Turbofan Engine During Cruise Turbofan failure during cruise, resulting in the loss of both thrust and electric power, is illustrated in the modified mission profile shown in Fig. 4, where the portions of flight using solely electric power are indicated in orange. Due to the significant thrust contribution from the turbofan, the aircraft would perform an emergency descent, allowing the aircraft to fly at the optimal altitude and velocity to an alternate airport.
